content_metadata.description: This video dives into the significance of Earth observation via remote sensing and satellites, highlighting the challenges and importance of continuing these efforts.

qAndA.answer: Remote sensing allows us to observe the Earth from a distance, providing a broader perspective and revealing the interconnectedness of different systems.
qAndA.question: What is the main benefit of remote sensing compared to traditional on-the-ground observations?

qAndA.answer: Satellites can observe the entire Earth, allowing scientists to collect data on a global scale and identify patterns that are not apparent from ground-based observations.
qAndA.question: Why are satellites particularly valuable for studying climate change?

qAndA.answer: A majority of the existing Earth-observing satellites are past their intended lifespan and could fail at any moment.
qAndA.question: What is the current state of Earth-observing satellites?

qAndA.answer: The GRACE mission uses two satellites to measure changes in Earth’s gravity field, allowing scientists to track water movement and understand how climate change is affecting water availability.
qAndA.question: What is the GRACE mission and why is it important?

qAndA.answer: The video starts with a curious and pensive tone but shifts to a more concerned and urgent mood as it highlights the challenges facing Earth observation and the potential consequences of losing valuable data.
qAndA.question: What is the overall mood of the video?

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Remote sensing is observing a medium, a process, some phenomenon without ever coming in direct
contact with that phenomenon.
So unlike a lab experiment or where you go to a place and make an in situ measurement,
we're actually touching the medium, remote sensing is observing it remotely from a distance.
And this actually provides a different kind of perspective on things.
When you're part of your medium, you're part of your experiment, you're part of the experience,
you get one perspective that's crucial.
You get a very different one when you're removed from it, when you're looking from space,
when you're looking from four or five hundred miles away or in some cases twenty thousand
miles away.
We can start up close, we can stand in a place and look at it, and we can zoom out.
And all of a sudden it takes on new meaning.
The trees are part of a broader system that sit on a landmass, that is a country that's
part of a continent that sits in an ocean.
And as we step back further and further and look at those same trees, we may not see
the leaves from far away, but we see the trees and how they fit into a broader earth system,
the clouds that surround them, the ice that's far north or far south of them, the oceans
that really are affecting the climate that is causing those trees to grow.
You know, satellites are really the best way to measure the effects of climate change,
because just one person on the ground and one place is very difficult to say of what
you see in front of you is due to climate change or due to some local phenomena or it's
just the weather.
And from space we can look at the Earth and we can integrate these observations of the
Earth and really make a better assessment about what's causing these changes and what
their long-term prognosis is.
A decade ago the Earth Observing System was beginning to be put in place.
A series of satellites designed to observe the Earth, take a snapshot of the Earth over
a period of years to understand its behavior.
Well, to date there are 14 Earth Observing satellites orbiting right now.
And of those 14, 13 are past their design life.
They're living on borrowed time and could go away at any moment.
I think funding is for these satellite missions is very much threatened right now.
There doesn't seem to be a lot of support in political circles right now for these missions
and so that's something that scientists were trying to do is to educate people about
why they're so important.
Like I said the Grace mission has been really in my opinion one of the best tools we have
for measuring the impacts of climate change on the Earth, it tells us where the water is
going and that's when we talk about climate change everybody thinks about the temperature
but it's really the water availability that's going to be the big impactor.
And so we'll be able to tell with Grace where we're losing water, where there's going
to be prolonged droughts, where there's going to be more flooding, where the ice is melting.
It's just this wonderful tool and now we're going to lose this tool for probably two to
three years.
And it's really unfortunate that we've kind of taken away one of our eyes in the sky.
The Earth is changing in ways that will affect our lives and just as we're realizing how
and why these changes are occurring, our ability to understand them is diminishing.
And frankly our future, our success in the future as a society really depends, is
to intimately link to our ability to anticipate what's coming.

youtube_description:
CIRES Fellow and NASA Chief Scientist Waleed Abdalati and CIRES Fellow Steve Nerem explain Remote Sensing and how it is used to study our planet.
